The authors present an R package named fpemlocal, a local implementation of a previously published global Bayesian hierarchical model. Similar functions are already available through an online version, but this R package may be more convenient for users who prefer the R interface and have unstable internet access. With the instructions from the article and README on GitHub, the package is user-friendly overall. Some suggestions for further improvement:
For use case 1.1, perhaps the package can directly include the results from a global run. The package only needs to extract the results for the country of interest to the user, instead of fitting a single-country model for the given country. Theoretically, by fixing non-country-specific parameters at the global FPEM estimates, the single-country implementation compromises the model accuracy. For use cases 1.2 and 1.3, the substantial saving in computational load overwhelms the slight loss in accuracy. But that does not apply to case 1.1.
Customize figure appearance. Current output figures are nice and clear, but they require some final minor changes if the user wants to include them in a presentation or a report. For example, replace variable names on axis titles with properly capitalized words. An easy way to achieve that is by changing the default setting and adding those arguments to the plot_fp_c function.
The users may need more instructions on preparing data for cases 1.2 and 1.3. The instructions should include column definitions and clarify which columns are mandatory.

Many researchers arrive at point in enrichment analysis where they have tables of enriched ontology terms and pathways, but don't know how to go beyond presenting those data as tables or perhaps bar graphs. The use of networks is an intuitive and powerful visualization option. The eXamine app for Cytoscape provides a nice approach for displaying a simplified version of enrichment results. A couple steps are missing, however, and a few minor edits are suggested.
Missing steps:
All sources of enrichment that I'm aware of provide rows of terms and a list of genes in a single field per row. It would be nice if you provided a bit of Python to transform that common input data type to that required by eXamine.
I was wondering about genes that belong to more than one term (often the case). I looks like your tool handles these via a piped list. Is that right? Please describe the correct syntax in the text so readers don't have to guess.
Minor suggestions:
Groups in Cytoscape are no longer provided as a separate plugin, but rather are now integrated into the core of Cytoscape. Your reference to "RBVI Cytoscape plugins" should be updated to simply mention the Cytoscape manual and point to the section on groups: http://manual.cytoscape.org/en/stable/Creating_Networks.html#grouping-nodes
The LaTeX formatting for your Python code is unfortunately rendering single quotes in a way that throws SyntaxError in Python. Can you update the rendering so one can simply copy/paste snippets?
In the next version of this paper, I'd highly recommend using py2cytoscape ( https://github.com/cytoscape/py2cytoscape). This will make the code you have write much more concise and easier to maintain or adapt. Likewise, I'd really like to see R examples and you can leverage RCy3 to make that code easy to write as well ( http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/RCy3.html).

I would like to express my special thanks to the editors for providing me with the opportunity to review this manuscript.

Abstract Section:
Background: Write the objective of this study clearly to inform the readers what you want to accomplish through this bibliometric study.
In the method section, it was mentioned that five years were covered. Nevertheless, the coverage period is six years, from 2017 to 2022.
In the results, the author needs to reflect significant findings in the form of data observations retrieved from this study, as the abstract is a concise version (summary) of the manuscript.
Introduction Section Methods Section Results Discussion Section.
It was stated on page 4 that no bibliometric study was done earlier on this topic of study. However, several other studies have been found in the literature on similar lines of research. It would be better to state the research gap concerning the utility of bibliometric analysis focusing on online marking and brand awareness using various databases such as Scopus and WoS. In the introduction, the author has to justify why this study was conducted and what it attempts to fulfill (considering the gap identified by earlier studies).
Mention the study design adopted in the methods section.
Mention the key terms and Boolean operators used for electronic search criteria within the Scopus database. Also, include the Scopus query used to retrieve the data.
Mention the inclusion criteria used to screen documents to be included in the bibliographic analysis within the text under the search strategy.
It is essential to mention the date you carried out the search and downloaded the data since it could be replicated by other researchers in the same or other fields.
On page 6, under the bibliometric tool, add the software name Biblioshiny in Rstudio.
The authors did not mention the Scopus downloaded data type. (For example. CSV or BibTex). Mention it. Mention it.
Write a short note about the retrieved information studied to reflect on the Author, sources, and documents, as mentioned in Figure 2.
On page 8, it was mentioned that in Figure 4, the top 20 globally most cited documents can be seen. Sustainability, International Journal of Education, Journal of Advertising, (mismatch). This information does not match the figure-4 provided on page number 8. Correct and update it.
Mention the Author's Full name in Figures 7 and 8. It is recommended that a table showing the top 10 authors with their affiliation, frequency (number of documents), percentage (%) of publication concerning the total, and the total citations received by each Author be created.
Besides Figure 6, a table showing the top journals published documents related to online marketing and brand awareness for HEI by various authors between 2017 and 2022 would be desirable.
Besides Figure 9, it is recommended to create a table showing the top cited documents with their Digital Object Identifier (DOI), total citations received per document, and citations received per year for the clarity of the readers. You can take the top 10 highly cited documents.

This an excellent manuscript that summarizes an application of immersive qualitative research to characterize decision-makers and decision-making pathways to the sustainability of the VMMC program in Zambia. The authors have done an excellent job translating complex narrative data into a well-structured, digestible framework of decision-making in the context of Zambian VMMC programming. I only have a couple of reflections and comments for the authors to consider in a revised manuscript:
METHODS
- In their analysis, can the authors comment on the extent to which their synthesis was team-based? Who was involved specifically in the data synthesis? Was member checking used to help validate the emerging decision-making frameworks or data interpretations?
DISCUSSION
- Given the current uncertainties about the future of PEPFAR programming (especially for funding vital prevention services like VMMC), could the authors comment on the utility of such a framework in helping to guide a more rapid transition to program sustainability in this current funding environment?

1. Title
The title is generally clear and relevant to the study topic. However, it should be reconsidered to better reflect the actual research design and analytical relationships examined. The use of the term “Role” is somewhat vague, while the study actually examines correlation and statistical effects. A more precise title should identify the specific relationship between psychological pricing and consumer purchasing behavior and, if appropriate, the empirical context.
2. Abstract
The abstract provides a general overview of the study and reports the main findings. However, it needs substantial improvement in terms of scientific precision. The research gap, sampling technique, measurement procedure, and statistical methodology are not sufficiently explained. The abstract also appears to overstate the causal implications of the findings. Since the study is based on cross-sectional questionnaire data, causal expressions should be used cautiously.
3. Introduction
The introduction establishes the general relevance of psychological pricing and consumer behavior. Nevertheless, it is relatively descriptive and repetitive and does not establish a sufficiently convincing research gap. The authors should clearly explain what is unknown, inconsistent, or insufficiently examined in previous research and how the present study addresses that gap. The claim that the management of Al-Salam stores is not fully aware of the effects of psychological pricing appears to be based mainly on the researchers’ observations and requires stronger empirical or documentary support.
4. Research Problem
The research problem is clearly formulated; however, it remains largely practical rather than theoretically driven. Simply asking whether psychological pricing affects purchasing behavior is insufficient to establish a strong research problem for an international journal. The authors should formulate the problem around a clearly demonstrated gap in the existing literature, particularly conflicting findings, unexplored dimensions, contextual differences, or theoretical limitations.
5. Research Objectives and Hypotheses
The objectives and hypotheses are generally aligned with the research variables. However, the hypotheses are largely formulated as direct relationships without adequate theoretical justification. The use of the term “effect” is also problematic because the research design is cross-sectional and based on self-reported questionnaire data. The authors should either provide a stronger causal research design or use more appropriate terminology such as “association” or “relationship.”
6. Theoretical Framework
The theoretical framework is one of the major weaknesses of the manuscript. Although the study provides several definitions and descriptions of psychological pricing, the discussion remains largely descriptive rather than explanatory. The manuscript does not establish a strong theoretical mechanism explaining why and through what psychological processes pricing cues influence purchasing behavior.
The authors should substantially strengthen the theoretical foundation by incorporating an appropriate consumer-behavior theory and explaining the mechanism connecting psychological pricing dimensions to cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses. The framework should not simply list definitions and previous findings; it should develop a coherent theoretical argument leading to the proposed hypotheses.
The previous review also identified weak theoretical integration and insufficient engagement with recent consumer-behavior literature.
7. Literature Review
The literature review requires considerable restructuring. It currently focuses heavily on definitions and general benefits of psychological pricing rather than critically synthesizing previous empirical studies. The authors should compare previous studies according to context, variables, methodology, sample, findings, and limitations, and then demonstrate precisely how the present study differs.
Greater use of recent international literature, particularly studies published during 2024–2026, is necessary. The existing literature base does not sufficiently demonstrate the novelty or international relevance of the study.
8. Methodology
The use of a descriptive-analytical approach and questionnaire survey is generally appropriate for an exploratory empirical study. However, the methodological description is not sufficiently detailed for replication.
The authors should clarify: The study states that 400 questionnaires were distributed and 288 valid questionnaires were analyzed, but the sampling process and selection procedure require substantially greater methodological clarification.
the exact sampling technique;
the characteristics of the target population;
the justification for the sample size;
the criteria for inclusion and exclusion;
the reasons for excluding the 112 questionnaires;
the development and sources of questionnaire items;
whether established measurement scales were adopted or developed;
the pilot study procedure;
procedures for content validity;
reliability and construct validity testing.
9. Measurement Validity and Reliability
This is a major methodological concern. The manuscript should provide sufficient evidence for the reliability and validity of the measurement model.
In particular, the authors should report and interpret, where applicable: Simply reporting that a questionnaire was measured using a five-point Likert scale is not sufficient to establish measurement quality.
Cronbach’s alpha;
Composite Reliability;
Average Variance Extracted (AVE);
convergent validity;
discriminant validity;
factor loadings;
appropriate model-fit indices.
10. Statistical Analysis
The statistical analysis requires careful re-examination. The manuscript reports AMOS V24 results, including β, R², C.R., and p-values. However, several inconsistencies appear between the narrative and the statistical tables.
For example, the terminology used for the pricing dimensions is inconsistent, including expressions such as “fractional prices,” “decimal prices,” “price separator,” “price line size,” and “price font size.” These inconsistencies make it difficult to determine whether the same constructs are being measured and tested throughout the manuscript.
The authors should carefully audit all tables, variable labels, coefficients, statistical values, and corresponding textual interpretations. This issue is particularly important because statistical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported findings.
11. SEM/AMOS Model
If AMOS and structural equation modeling are being used, the manuscript should provide the complete measurement and structural model assessment. Reporting regression coefficients and p-values alone is insufficient.
The authors should report appropriate model-fit indices, such as:
χ²/df, CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, and other relevant indicators, together with acceptable thresholds and interpretation.
The manuscript should also distinguish clearly between the measurement model and the structural model.
12. Extremely High Correlations and R²
The reported relationships are unusually strong. For example, the overall correlation between psychological pricing and consumer purchasing behavior is reported as 0.91, while R² is reported as 0.82.
Such high values require additional methodological justification. The authors should investigate the possibility of: The manuscript should provide appropriate diagnostic tests rather than assuming that the high coefficients automatically demonstrate a strong substantive effect.
conceptual overlap between constructs;
common method bias;
multicollinearity;
insufficient discriminant validity;
item redundancy.
13. Results and Discussion
The results are presented in relation to the hypotheses, which is useful. However, the discussion mainly repeats the statistical findings rather than critically interpreting them.
The authors should explain: The discussion should therefore move beyond “the hypothesis was accepted” toward a deeper theoretical and empirical interpretation.
why the findings occurred;
how they compare with previous studies;
why they agree or disagree with previous findings;
what theoretical implications arise from the results;
what contextual factors in the Iraqi retail environment might explain the findings.
14. Causality
A major concern is the repeated use of causal language. The study uses a cross-sectional questionnaire and self-reported responses, which can demonstrate statistical associations but cannot, by themselves, establish strong causal relationships.
Statements implying that psychological pricing causes purchasing behavior, increases sales, increases profits, or increases market share should therefore be substantially moderated unless direct longitudinal, experimental, or financial evidence is provided.
15. Conclusions
The conclusions generally correspond to the statistical findings, but some conclusions extend beyond what was actually measured.
In particular, the manuscript links psychological pricing to increased sales, profits, and market share, although these outcomes were not directly measured in the study. This represents an important inferential leap. The conclusions should be restricted to the variables actually investigated.
16. Recommendations
The recommendations have practical relevance, but several are too general and repetitive. They should be more directly derived from the empirical findings.
The authors should distinguish between recommendations supported directly by the results and suggestions requiring further empirical verification. For example, claims that psychological pricing increases organizational profits or market share should not be presented as established findings when financial or market-share data were not collected.
17. References
The reference list requires improvement in terms of recency, consistency, and international coverage. The authors should incorporate substantially more recent peer-reviewed studies and ensure that all references directly support the claims for which they are cited.
The manuscript also needs consistent reference formatting and careful verification of bibliographic information.
18. Language and Academic Writing
The manuscript requires extensive English-language editing. There are repeated grammatical problems, awkward expressions, inconsistent terminology, unnecessary repetition, and instances that appear to reflect literal or mechanical translation.
The terminology for the same constructs should be standardized throughout the manuscript. This issue was also explicitly identified in the previous peer-review report.

Stankovic et al assessed the factors associated with mentioning academic degrees on the journal’s title page. The current study is interesting and sheds a light on an important topic, although the authors chose a restricted sample to analyze (i.e. high impact medical journals). I believe that the current report can be improved by clarifying some points within its methods section, as follows.
In the methods section, the authors did not define “academic degrees”. In the data associated with this study, they included columns on “Academic degrees”, “job titles”, and “fellowship designations”. In medicine, reporting of fellowships might be more important than the academic degree, especially if the researcher is a clinician working in a non-academic institution. The authors should clearly define what they mean by “academic degree” that they used in their analysis.
In the methods section, the authors categorized journals according to specialty as general or specific. The authors should detail the basis of this classification. Moreover, the authors categorized open access status into yes, no, or partly, where “partly” is not a common word used to describe the open access status (examples of common, well-defined words include green open access, hybrid access and so on). By going back to the data, I observed several non-open access journals categorized as “partly”, so I would suggest adopting strict criteria for categorization, such as the one suggested by Scopus:
“Open Access Journals are indicated as Open Access if the journal is listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and/or the Directory of Open Access Scholarly Resources (ROAD)”.
In the discussion section, the authors should include studies that discussed the impact of an academic degree in publishing, which would complement the points raised by the authors in the present report.

This paper describes a pilot study protocol for a multi-site AMR surveillance project, which aims to prospectively link clinical and diagnostic microbiological data and which can be implemented alongside routine clinical care. The study has gained ethical approval and the pilot phase is ongoing.
The type of prospective AMR surveillance described by this protocol is much needed and, as the authors identify, should help to minimise the biases associated with many AMR studies which are frequently pathogen/drug specific, or which do not link microbiology to clinical data. The site-level data dashboard is a great development which will provide user-friendly and interactive data visualisation.
p4-5: The authors begin to address this in the discussion, but is the definition of HAI/CAI too narrow/specific? Will this approach miss patients who have attended other types of healthcare setting than acute care hospitals - for example outpatient services and health centres? Likewise, will definition of community acquired be able to distinguish community onset/hospital acquired from true community onset infections? The extended data describes possible reclassification of some CA cases based on transfer and admission dates. Although standardisation across sites may be difficult, the authors might consider making a judgement on this classification prospectively at enrolment and taking into account more nuanced clinical history.
p5: Likewise, It's not completely clear whether a blood culture collected within 24 hours of admission (CAI) automatically put someone in CAI category?
p5: What will be the purpose of qSOFA and sepsis six in the analysis? It is extremely challenging to come up with a unifying sepsis severity score for all age groups, particularly in LMICs where qSOFA is not well validated, but may be worth highlighting these limitations in the discussion if sepsis severity will play an important role in the burden models. Will any blood tests be taken into account?
General/Methods: A lot of information on methods is contained comprehensively within the SOPs in extended data. Whilst appreciating the word count limitations, could some of these be summarised in the main paper - in particular? Minor comments:
Cost data could be more comprehensively described - is it only antibiotics included in the unit costs and are these healthcare direct costs or patient indirect costs as well?
Likewise, the qualitative aspect to this study will be hugely informative but the description of this is somewhat hidden in the main text. Could this be separated out and made clearer in the confines of the work count?
Discussion p 8: "The effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the diagnostic stewardship activities will be monitored as the proportion of cases with linked diagnostic specimens." How does this address cost-effectiveness? Again could this be made clearer in a costing paragraph in methods?
Are there any references for paragraph two of the introduction, which describes the various biases associated with existing AMR surveillance data?
What level of QC is available to the diagnostic laboratories?
How were surveillance wards selected? Any space to explain this in the main text?
Why were the specific target pathogens chosen? If possible a justification would be informative.

The authors provide a comprehensive review for an important, yet complex disease. Still, the text is clear and easy to read – both for non-experts and new researchers. In this review, Abuga et al. bring together the fields knowledge of severe anemia, iron deficiency, and invasive bacterial infections. While the list of comorbidities which are associated with invasive bacterial infection is long and well documented ( e.g. malnutrition, malaria, HIV, SCD), the authors instead focus on one aspect, anaemia.
They approach this review by discussing the impact of anemia on iron metabolism, followed by a cell by cell breakdown of both innate and adaptive immune cells. Each paragraph/section could be expanded into its own review. Yet, the authors provide a good summary here. As the authors state, the current data the mechanism(s) of these interactions is incomplete.
Rather than delving into the details between studies, the authors bring together data for the wider picture. Further, the complexities of the aetiologies for the population at risk would make this comparison difficult, in such a broad review as this. Still, I personally enjoyed the information provided in the tables. For example, Table 1 highlights discrepancies in the data – where the definition of severe anemia can vary and the association with malaria not reported.
I think the review is well structured and timely, and drives the message that a more comprehensive understanding is needed, particularly in future prospective clinical studies.

Summary of the manuscript: The manuscript presents a bibliometric analysis of research on functional ingredients used in developing functional biscuits. It aims to identify current trends, prolific authors, influential articles, and potential future advancements in this research area. The analysis is based on 395 articles retrieved from the Scopus database between 2013 and 2023, employing tools like R Studio and VOS Viewer for performance analysis and science mapping.
Overall assessment: The manuscript is well-structured and presents an important analysis of the literature on functional ingredients and their application in biscuits. The methodology is clear, and the use of bibliometric tools is appropriate for the research objectives. However, there are some areas that need improvement to enhance the clarity and impact of the paper.
Major comments: Minor comments: Recommendation:
Literature review:
The literature review should be expanded to provide a more comprehensive background on the importance of functional biscuits and their role in health. The current review is somewhat brief and does not adequately establish the context for the bibliometric analysis.
There should be more discussion on the different types of functional ingredients commonly used in biscuit formulations and their specific health benefits.
Methodology:
The selection criteria for articles should be explained in more detail. While the use of the SPAR-4-SLR method is mentioned, the manuscript does not clearly describe how the articles were filtered and selected beyond the initial database search. It would be beneficial to include a flowchart illustrating the selection process.
The manuscript claims that the SPAR-4-SLR method is superior to PRISMA guidelines but does not provide evidence or references to support this claim. A comparison or justification for this choice would strengthen the methodology section.
Data analysis:
While the results section is thorough, it would benefit from more interpretation of the data. For instance, the manuscript mentions trends in publication growth and the most cited articles but does not discuss why these trends are occurring or their implications for the field.
The network analysis section should include a discussion on the significance of the clusters identified and how they relate to the development of functional biscuits.
Discussion and conclusion:
The discussion should be expanded to include the implications of the findings for future research and industry practice. Specifically, how can the identified trends and gaps be addressed in future studies? What are the practical applications of these findings in the food industry?
The conclusion section is brief and could be more robust. It should summarize the key findings and suggest actionable recommendations for researchers and practitioners.
Clarity and readability:
Some parts of the manuscript are densely written and could benefit from clearer language and shorter sentences. Simplifying the presentation of the data, particularly in the results section, would make the manuscript more accessible to a broader audience.
The use of figures and tables is appropriate, but some could be better integrated into the text. For example, the discussion could reference specific tables or figures more explicitly to guide the reader.
Abstract: The abstract provides a good summary of the paper, but it could be more specific about the key findings and their implications.
References: Ensure all references are current and relevant. Some of the references cited are over a decade old, and it might be beneficial to include more recent studies to support the analysis.
Formatting: Check for consistency in formatting, particularly in the references section and the use of headings and subheadings.
Data presentation: Remove the percentage signs if individual counting is being referred to or ensure the percentages are correct. For instance, the statement "Publications as review papers constitute 61% and 1% as conference papers" needs clarification or correction.
Language: Correct typographical errors in the conclusion, such as changing "It study shows" to "This study shows."
The manuscript has potential and provides valuable insights into the research trends on functional ingredients in biscuits. However, it requires significant revisions to improve the depth of analysis, clarity of presentation, and overall impact. I recommend a major revision before reconsideration for publication.
If this is a Living Systematic Review, is the ‘living’ method appropriate and is the search schedule clearly defined and justified? (‘Living Systematic Review’ or a variation of this term should be included in the title.)
Not applicable

Thank you for inviting me to review this protocol. Overall, it is well written. Below are my comments to improve the readability of the protocol and rigour of the intended review:
ABSTRACT INTRODUCTION CRITERIA FOR INCLUSION SEARCH METHODOLOGY DATA (AND SOFTWARE) AVAILABILITY STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS
Avoid conjunctive adverbs in abstracts “however” “therefore”…
See PRISMA extension for abstracts of systematic reviews to ensure that all elements of the review are being reported.
The use of “the” is redundant in several places for example “the findings will assist the development of” should read like “findings will assist in the development of”, “the review findings” (no need for “the”)…
A single statement of the aim is needed before the research questions.
The fact that the protocol is registered in PROSPERO is a strength. I query, however, the recency of this review given that the protocol was registered 16 months ago. Have there been any changes made to the protocol since?
It is unclear which framework is underpinning the criteria for inclusion. PICO? PIO? PEO? PCC? Etc. This must be made explicit and appropriate resource cited. Inclusion and exclusion criteria should then be reorganised accordingly.
I strongly encourage the authors to avoid the “English” database limit unless there is a strong reason to do so.
I now see that PICo will be used. Perhaps use the same framework to rework the criteria for inclusion.
Not sure if Table 1 adds anything not already covered under CRITERIA FOR INCLUSION.
I query whether Microsoft Excel is the best software to screen studies. I recommend using Covidence (if funding is available) as this is often the best and most user-friendly tool/online software to deduplicate records and conduct blinded screening at title, abstract, and full text screening stages and also extract data. If funding is not available for a Covidence license, I recommend the free online software Rayyan.
“To the best of the author’s knowledge” should read “To the best of the authors’ knowledge” since there is more than one author on this paper.
I see that you justified the English limiter here.

This study analyzed Salivary nitric oxide, Simplified Oral Hygiene Index, and salivary flow rate in smokers and non-smokers: a cross-sectional study. The issues identified are minor and with these minor revisions, the protocol should be ready for indexing and implementation.
Abstract Claims about dengue serotyping and formatting Aims and Objectives
In the Abstract, the eligibility criterion is written as “individuals aged >1 year,” whereas other sections use “aged ≥1 year.” Please choose one format (either “>” or “≥”) and apply it consistently throughout the manuscript.
Please explicitly state the main objective(s) of the study in the Background portion of the Abstract.
The statement: “To achieve this, this study will utilize a novel combination of antigens to assess exposure levels to multiple malaria species (P. falciparum, P. vivax and P. knowlesi) and dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4).” raises a concern. Please clarify whether the proposed platform can reliably differentiate dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4). The currently cited studies (14–16, 28) do not appear to support serotype-level discrimination, based on the information provided. Please confirm and revise the claim as needed. Or any available study assessing its performance compared to serotyping PCR.
In addition, “DENV-1” to “DENV-4” should not be italicized.
The sentence: “Similarly, recently published studies have shown that specific dengue antigens can identify serotypes of past infection and can be used to study serotype-specific exposures and transmission dynamics.17” Please support this statement with at least two appropriate references.
In Objective (c), the phrase “RDT-based incidence” appears conceptually inconsistent with a cross-sectional design, which typically estimates prevalence rather than incidence. If incidence is intended, please specify the follow-up structure (e.g., repeated measurements over time) and clearly describe how incidence will be measured. If repeated assessments are not planned, consider revising “incidence” to “prevalence” (or an equivalent cross-sectional measure) for accuracy.
Table 1
The title of Table 1 should be expanded to be more complete and self-explanatory (i.e., understandable without referring extensively to the main text).
Study area definitions
In the sentence, “Sites will represent areas with a high burden of malaria and dengue, varying levels of deforestation…”, please define “high burden” and “varying levels of deforestation” more explicitly in this section. For example, specify the data source and threshold(s) used to categorize burden, and the metric(s) used to quantify deforestation (and how categories are determined).
Figure 1 (map clarity)
Figure 1: The map is somewhat confusing. It is unclear what the dark green color represents—does it indicate tree cover? If so, what does the surrounding lighter area represent (e.g., grassland )? It is uncertain whether such clear boundaries between trees and grass actually exist on the ground as depicted in the map.
Subheading wording
Consider renaming the subheading “Sample size” to “Sample size and sampling method” to better reflect the content and improve readability.
Redundancy in consent description
In the Serological Surveys section, the paragraph describing written informed consent appears to repeat information already provided in the Ethical Considerations section. Please consider condensing the text and/or referring back to the Ethics section to reduce redundancy while maintaining clarity.

Cohen and Marron present a concept of evolution that centers on interactions on different level - molecular, cellular, organismal etc. - which are perceived as a universal anti-entropic force. Entropy is understood as a tendency for increasing disorder and is viewed as the principal selective factor in evolution. The antientropic evolution is postulated to be 'universal', hence no neutral evolutionary processes. The authors, then, forward the principle of 'survival of the fitted' whereby all biological entities that counter entropy with sufficient success to remain in an ordered state survive.
Although not exactly new (indeed, it goes back to Boltzmann who the authors duly cite!), the notion of the fundamental nature of the antientropic tendencies in evolution is worth putting forward. More specifically, the emphasis on interactions permeating the entire biological organization as a universal antientropic factor is worthy and might appeal to many biologists as a fresh perspective eon the general character of evolution..
However, I find several areas within and around these where concepts where I feel compelled to mount criticisms, and not altogether minor ones.
First, to me, the 'survival of the fitted' appears to be a non sequitur. Let us say, everything is fine with entropy as a selective factor and interactions, but why not survival of the fittest, that is, those that counteract entropy most efficiently and, as a result, leave more progeny than others?
Second, in all their discussion of entropy, the authors refer only to classical,equilibirum thermodynamics. As far as I can see, this discussion cannot be complete without taking into account the concepts of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, in particular, maximization of entropy production and dissipative structures. The literature on these subjects is extensive, starting with Prigogine.
Third, to me, it is inexplicable how and why, when discussing the pivotal roles of interactions at different levels in evolution, the authors fail to include Maynard Smith-Szathmary's concept of major transitions in evolution (Ref. 1 1 and references therein) and, especially, the generalized form of this concept that comes uncannily close to the concept of interactions-driven evolution discussed here 2.
Fourth, I believe that, along with the key role of interaction, it is essential for developing a general concept of evolution, to consider competition between interactions on different scales and the resulting frustrated states 2.
Finally, more with respect to the presentation of the material. The figures in the current manuscript are over-simplified and, overall, underwhelming. Figure 1 is a trivial illustration of the concept of entropy and is superfluous (readers unfamiliar with the second law will not benefit from reading this article) whereas for Figures 2 and 3, more elaborate schemes are advisable.

This article is highly relevant and innovative because it highlights the integration of AI games and deep learning in inclusive education, particularly for students with Specific Learning Disorders (SLD). It is supported by a strong and comprehensive theoretical foundation, a systematic writing structure, and in-depth analysis through a qualitative, literature-based approach, resulting in a clear and applicable conceptual framework. This article also provides practical contributions in the form of recommendations for teachers, schools, and policymakers. Several areas for improvement include the need for empirical data or field trials so that findings are not merely conceptual and can demonstrate effectiveness in real terms. The limitations of the method should not only use literature studies, which are susceptible to interpretation bias, and the still minimal discussion of technical implementation in the classroom (for example, details of the actual use of AI), so that the resulting conclusions show more potential than strong evidence.

The authors present an interesting work for predicting cancer cells drug responses based on " the gene expression profile of 47 genes representing significant hubs in pan cancer transcriptomes" from untreated cells lines. The approach is original, as they did not select a specific set of genes from drug sensitivity experiments, but proposed " an unbiased discovery approach, motivated by the hypothesis that co-expression network hubs encode useful information for investigating drug response in vitro " . Next, they investigated co-expression network hubs and drug responses and validated their approach using independant data sets including cell line-drug data.
The study is well conceived and executed. The approaches used are suitable, and the description of work is adequately detailed. Data are clearly presented, and for the most part conclusions are reasonable. The method appears interesting, I think the paper would be a nice contribution that will be well-cited. Despite the difficulty of comparison, prediction performance of the model was compared to existing published methods and shows comparable results. Moreover the manuscript is well written.
The authors need to clarify on the following points:
Figure1:
It will be better to specify the type of data (microarrays?) and source (CCLE?) in input for "transcriptomic data from untreated cell lines".
Methods, page 4 :
The reason why removal of genes is needed is not clear: "Although lasso or elastic net regularizations are also suitable approaches, they would have required the estimation of additional learning parameters and the removal of genes, which were deemed biologically interesting before model training......."
Methods, page 5 (line 24) :
The authors should specify what they mean by " the original data" which kind of files they used (raw data, gene counts ...). (line 28: RNS-seq instead of RNA-seq).
Results, page 9:
Could the authors specify if drugs with nearest clusters or CI values belong to a same drug "class" or not? Is there a relationship between performance prediction and drug classes?
Results, page 9:
This sentence is not clear: " As the GDSC dataset shares "different" cell lines in common with CCLE..."
Results, page 12:
" However elastic net model required 613 genes as input features": Does this set include the 47-hub model genes?
Discussion, page 14:
Prediction performance and cancer types is discussed, what about "hematopoietic and lymphoid tissues"? This cancer type seems to strongly differ from other types in their drug responses and gene expression (see Figures 2 and 4). Could the authors comment on these data?
Discussion, page 16:
" Nevertheless future work could benefit from the incorporation of other "omics" data .. CCLE RNA-seq dataset could allow the analysis of transcript-level ( gene isoform)". However RNA-seq technology has a larger potential than extracting transcript isoform and allows to extract genomic (mutation, indels, gene fusion, ...) and transcriptomic events (gene expression, splice variant, non-coding RNA), could the authors enlarge their comment about this potential and their prediction method? Also what about epigenetics data to predict drug sensitivity?

This well-written review article covers the translation of the molecular clock mechanism for health and healthy aging, which is an important topic in the field. I strongly support the publication of this article, and a brief description of the following points would be useful for further understanding:
Are the therapeutic effects of nobiletin dependent on both RORα and RORγ? As the authors described, isoforms of REV-ERB (α and β) and ROR (α, β, and γ) have different expression patterns and physiological functions. Therefore, it would be nice to discuss the possibility and potential of isoform-selective ligands as well.
Because nobiletin is a natural compound and other REV-ERB/ROR ligands are synthetic compounds, it would be nice to mention the merit (and demerit) of natural compounds compared to synthetic compounds.
Minor points:
Page 4, line 2: Drosophila to be italic.
Page 5, “Therapeutic relevance of REV-ERBs and RORs” section, lines 2-3: “expression” is duplicated.
Page 6, line 11: ZT may need an explanation.
Page 6, the second paragraph, line 1: Rev-erba-/- to be italic.
Please check whether references 60 (Emery and Clayton, 2001) and 137 (Nagoshi et al., 2004) are proper literature in the context.

The report addresses a relevant and analytically interesting case, provides useful coverage of the main political actors, and offers a promising basis for comparative analysis.
Here are some suggestions for further improvement:
1. The last part of the introduction ("While populism in Montenegro is not as deeply entrenched as elsewhere, it is increasingly invoked in elite competition and identity-based mobilization targeting EU influence") may raise further questions. The authors should clarify this argument in an additional 1–2 sentences.
2. The second paragraph of the second part seems out of context. It may be difficult for readers to understand the connection between the parties listed here and those discussed separately later. It is worth noting that the following section addresses both populist parties that have entered parliament and extra-parliamentary populist actors.
3.It would enhance clarity to group the parties presented in Part 2 by criteria such as the type of populist message they convey (for example, the first group could include radical right-wing populists, while the second could focus on valence populists). This organisation would offer readers a more comprehensive picture of populist party actors rather than a fragmented one. Moreover, it may be challenging for readers to differentiate between opposition and government parties. Clearly indicating this in the chapter would provide a more structured framework for the report.
4. The cases discussed in Part 3 are well-analyzed; however, the presence of many different actors may lead to a loss of systematic coherence in the report. Once again, it would be better to present these six parties in relation to the nexus between Euroscepticism and populism.
5. The report should also clarify whose (domestic political parties, state institutions, civil society, the EU, or the broader accession framework) responses are being analysed in Part 4. Currently, these levels are mixed. It is essential to distinguish among party-based, institutional, and EU-level responses.
6. The report also needs to be more cautious about its claims of effectiveness (Hence, the most effective response to populism and Euroscepticism in Montenegro is...).Claims that media resilience, targeted EU communication, or the EU Growth Plan mitigate Euroscepticism should be supported by evidence or presented more carefully as plausible mechanisms rather than established findings.
7. A conclusion should highlight that Montenegro is a case in which populist actors use EU-related discourse for domestic competition, while the goal of EU accession remains the primary strategic objective. This positions Montenegro differently from other cases.
8. As Montenegro is an EU candidate country, it would have been better to draw on existing literature on Euroscepticism and populism in EU candidate states, particularly since the paper centres on EU conditionality.

Review
This article analyses how digitalization has transformed political participation among young adults in contemporary Europe.
The article is well written and well-grounded in relevant literature. It addresses a question that is important to the study of digital politics today.
The literature review in the background section is well written. It presents works that have analysed digital participation of young people in Europe.
The paper uses a qualitative meta-analysis of relevant research conducted about young adults’ and digital participation in Europe. The “Method” section explains the paper’s methodology.
The selection of relevant articles has been explained in a feasible manner:
“In terms of data collection, a thorough literature review was performed utilizing the Web of Science database. The investigation encompassed the timeframe from 2014 to 2025 and exclusively featured peer-reviewed academic publications authored in English. Search keywords encompassed combinations of digitalization, youth, political engagement, Europe, e-democracy, and online activism. The inclusion criteria mandated that each study (a) concentrate on European contexts, (b) examine digital tools or platforms concerning political engagement, and (c) encompass youth populatons aged 15–35.“
What I think would be helpful in the methodology section is a table that gives an overview of all 30 papers that were identified, giving an ID to each, and mentioning the following information for each paper in a separate column:
ID (1, 2, … 30)
Authors
Publication year
Journal title
Main research question
Methodology
Number of citations thus far in Web of Science
Date of access (Web of Science)
This would help giving the reader an immediate overview of what papers were included in the meta-analysis.
The “Results” section presents the results of the analysis. The presentation is insightful and well written. However, I was not always sure what statements were derived from the 30 papers and which one from other works (e.g. Eurostat 2025).
I recommend that more references are added to the results section and that the author uses paper IDs (1, 2, … 30) that refer to a table papers included in the meta-analysis. It then becomes evident to the reader what information in the results section has been derived from what papers included in the meta-analysis. Furthermore, I think it would be advantageous to indicate what information has been derived from more than one paper. Recurrent findings that we can find in many papers is the most relevant insights one can gain from a meta-analysis.
Conclusion: The results have been well summarised. I do, however, think that the author could more pinpoint the most central findings by adding a list of 3-5 bullet points that summarise the main findings about young people’s digital political participation in Europe that were recurrent in the papers included in the meta-analysis.
Overall, the findings are interesting and the paper is well written. They can be presented in a better way than at the moment.
My recommendation is:
Approve with Reservations

As the breadth of CHIM studies expands, notably to LMIC settings, this is a timely case study-based framework for inclusion of participants from vulnerable groups (in this case PLHIV). The article is reasonable well written, nicely structured and easily accessible to experts and those entering the field of CHIM research. It covers some new ground and is a helpful addition to the literature. However, whilst posing many questions, the paper does not always provide the answers. For example, differences in the financial circumstances of PLHIV are noted, potentially at odds with the local recommendation for a standard reimbursement rate irrespective of vulnerabilities (Ref 31). How was this difference in views reconciled? The manuscript also suffers a little from poor editing, with numerous grammatical errors. These should be corrected for final indexing.
I have a few minor comments that the authors could also consider:
Introduction – was the “feedback” from PPIE sessions formalised through a qualitative research study design or just informal? Please specify.
Table 1
Q 1
Ethical– does “population affected” refer only to participants or also to the community, given PLHIV may be highly infectious? Please clarify and expand statement as necessary
Considerations – perhaps an additional point is “what alternate strategies to answer the question have been considered”?
Q2
Considerations – maybe a little off base, but "reputational risk to CHIM research" could also be considered here
Risk and burden to individual participants
para 2 of this section indicates participants are “housed … in single-occupancy study accommodation”. This might be read as rather punitive without some further indication of duration of confinement, facilities available etc

This study has evaluated antibacterial efficacy of a colloidal silver gel against three important oral bacteria. In context of the currently available dentifrice products not being full effective in preventing the widespread problem of dental caries, need and research for new more effective dentifrices is justified. Their idea of assaying the test gel not only against individual bacteria, but also against the mixed-species is a logical one, as that represents real-life situations a bit more closely. In the recent past, maintenance of good oral health has been shown to be important for good cardiovascular health, healthy pregnancy, etc.
They may consider re-framing the last sentence of the third paragraph in 'Introduction'. They may also check for correct placement of all references; For e.g. references 2-3 have been cited in first paragraph in an oral health context, but their titles seem to be more relevant to wound management.
While, I do not have any reservations in recommending this article in its present form for indexing, I suggest for following additional experiments for future studies by these authors:
Effect of this gel on pre-formed biofilms of oral bacteria should be checked on two different parameters i.e. whether this gel can kill bacteria in biofilm, and whether it can eradicate the pre-formed biofilm with/without killing the bacteria in it.
Results of current study indicate their gel to possess a bactericidal action. They may consider extending the incubation till 48-72 hours after transferring the gel-exposed bacteria onto fresh gel-free media, to confirm the true bactericidal effect, and absence of post-antibiotic effect (PAE).
They may consider determination of MIC, MBC, and time required to kill. The latter is important as typical dentifrice products like mouthwashes/toothpaste get few seconds/minutes to exert their effect in the mouth.
It will be interesting to investigate whether at sub-inhibitory concentrations their product can reduce lactic acid production by the Streptococci, which is a major virulence factor involved in demineralization of teeth. Whether sub-inhibitory concentrations can inhibit quorum-sensing in these bacteria?
In the current study, cellulose discs were used as surface for biofilm formation. In future studies, they may consider some material similar to teeth-substance (e.g. calcium) as the surface for biofilm formation.

The manuscript is generally well-written, with an appropriate length and adequate language use. The methodology is acceptable, and it is commendable that the authors have registered their review protocol in PROSPERO.
Overall, I find the manuscript suitable for acceptance. However, a few minor revisions are necessary to enhance manuscript clarity.
Minor Revisions:
The baseline characteristics of the included studies should be described in more detail. It would be valuable to include variables such as the mean age of participants, gender distribution, hospital setting, and patient ethnicity or geographical background to provide better context of the participants.
Given the operator-dependent nature of ultrasound, the reviewer suggests the authors specify who performed the ultrasound-guided SWL in the included studies — for instance, whether it was a urologist, a radiologist, or a trained nurse.
There appears to be notable heterogeneity in the outcomes related to SFR and complication rates. The authors might consider exploring additional sources of this heterogeneity through subgroup analyses beyond age group — for example, by stratifying according to stone location (e.g., upper pole, renal pelvis), the number of sessions, or variations in energy and frequency settings used during shockwave lithotripsy.
In terms of complications, it is unclear whether the analysis refers to overall complications or specific categories. If feasible, a subgroup analysis for individual complications (e.g., hematuria, steinstrasse) would provide valuable insights. If such analysis cannot be performed, the authors should consider addressing this as a limitation.
If this is a Living Systematic Review, is the ‘living’ method appropriate and is the search schedule clearly defined and justified? (‘Living Systematic Review’ or a variation of this term should be included in the title.)

This is a very interesting and important article looking at the ability of Community Pharmacists and Patent Proprietary Medicine Vendors in two states of Nigeria to provide FP that meets the needs of those seeking it. Specifically, the research examines whether the fertility intentions of women in the sample can predict contraceptive continuation.
Specific comments:
It would be helpful to mention who funds the IntegratE project.
A table presenting the information found in the study sites would help guide the reader through all the data. You could then add a bit of information about demographic similarities/differences of the two states, including information about religion, wealth quintile, etc., to help readers who are unfamiliar with Nigeria. As I read further, your sample seems highly educational and with high employment rates. Does your sample reflect the employment and educational averages for the states, or is this a factor of where they sought their FP?
Why no mention of the finding of those who did not report on side effects as being less likely to be using contraception at follow-up?
Are you missing an "and" after (Protocol 878)?
I'm confused about Figure 3. It seems like it should come higher up in the results. I'm also confused about an n of 411 in Figure 3 (the number asked about their fertility intentions), but when you break down fertility intentions by continuation in figure 2, you have a higher n (n=491). Is the difference being asked fertility intentions by the data collector vs. the provider (CP or PPMV)? If so, that could be made more clear to the reader. Is it being used as a proxy for quality of care? Were other proxy indicators for quality of care collected, such as counseling on side effects?
I'm also confused as to why having been asked about their fertility intentions by the provider was not included as an independent variable. In the discussion you highlight the importance of discussing fertility intentions during counseling, but this is not a variable I see listed in your analysis. The same is true of providing information about side effects. I don't see this variable in your model, but you mention its importance in the discussion.
I recommend clarification on the last two points to ensure that the discussion and conclusions flow from the results.

Morales et al. provide a robust investigation of social annotation in the context of higher education by looking at 3 different undergraduate courses from 3 different disciplines. The large number of annotations analysed suggests that the results may be valid in many other educational contexts. The contextualisation of the research within an existing scholarly tradition is very accurate and the choice of using an established protocol (codebook) for qualitative research is excellent for the comparability of the results.
The discussion and interpretation are appropriate and rightfully acknowledge limitations that can occur in field studies and prevented the researchers to gain more detailed insight.
An important issue that is not clear from the article is whether informed consent has been obtained from the students. Moreover, it is not possible to fully reproduce the results of the study because the full text of the annotations is missing.
A few smaller remarks that could improve the presentation of the research:
Given the inconsistencies between academic calendars in various countries and the differences between Northern and Southern hemisphere, it would be better to express the time range of the data collection in number of weeks and months of the year. Now it is only stated: winter 2019 semester.
In place of Table 4, Figure 3 could be modified by using stacked bars to show the proportion of annotations for each course within each bar (e.g. 3 different shades of orange for no-thread)

Reviewer Report
This manuscript addresses an important and frequently misunderstood aspect of health professions education (HPE) research: sample size determination across different study designs. The authors should be commended for attempting to consolidate dispersed methodological guidance into a single practical resource tailored to HPE researchers. The manuscript is well structured, clearly written, and likely to be useful for novice researchers, reviewers, and educators.
However, although presented as a "methodology guide", the manuscript is largely a narrative synthesis of existing recommendations rather than a formal methodological framework. Some recommendations are presented too definitively despite being based on rules of thumb rather than universally accepted methodological standards. In addition, several important methodological nuances are simplified or omitted. Addressing these issues would substantially improve the scientific rigor and long-term usefulness of the guide.
Major comments
1. Clarify the methodology used to develop this guide
The manuscript describes itself as a methodology guide, yet it is not clear how the guidance was developed.
The authors cite statistical textbooks, methodological papers and HPE literature, but there is no description of: Consequently, readers cannot determine whether this represents: Recommendation
how references were identified,
whether literature was systematically searched,
whether guidance was selected using predefined criteria,
how conflicting recommendations were reconciled.
an expert narrative review,
a consensus document,
or a structured methodological synthesis.
Include a brief Methods section describing: This would considerably strengthen the credibility of the guide.
literature sources
search strategy (if applicable)
selection approach
rationale for included recommendations
2. Some recommendations are presented too prescriptively
Throughout the manuscript, certain sample size recommendations are written as if they are universally accepted.
Examples include: These are useful practical benchmarks but remain context-dependent.
12 participants per group for pilot studies
30 participants for Cronbach alpha
10 participants per questionnaire item
≥200 for CFA
9–20 interviews for qualitative research
Modern methodological literature increasingly discourages rigid numerical thresholds.
The manuscript should consistently emphasise that these values are illustrative guidance rather than minimum methodological requirements.
3. More discussion is needed regarding software implementation
The guide frequently refers to formulas but provides relatively little practical guidance regarding modern software.
Most HPE researchers now calculate sample size using software rather than manual equations.
Consider briefly discussing: A table matching study designs with commonly used software would substantially improve practical usability.
G*Power
R packages (pwr, simr)
PASS
Stata
SAS
4. Limited discussion of complex contemporary HPE study designs
The manuscript appropriately covers common designs but could acknowledge several increasingly common HPE designs, including: Even if detailed formulas are beyond scope, acknowledging these designs and directing readers to appropriate resources would improve completeness.
mixed-methods studies
longitudinal cohort studies
adaptive educational trials
Bayesian approaches
non-inferiority educational studies
equivalence testing
multilevel mixed-effects educational research
5. Greater emphasis on estimation rather than significance testing
Current methodological guidance increasingly recommends planning studies around estimation precision (confidence interval width) rather than solely statistical power.
Although the manuscript discusses power extensively, confidence-interval-based planning receives relatively limited attention.
A short section discussing estimation-based sample size planning would modernize the guide.
Minor comments
6. Table 1 could be improved
Table 1 is very useful but could become an even stronger quick-reference resource.
Consider adding columns for:
primary statistical analysis
commonly used software
important assumptions
common pitfalls
7. Effect size section
The discussion regarding effect size is excellent.
However, it would help readers if the manuscript also briefly discussed:
minimally important educational differences
educational versus statistical significance
why published effect sizes should be interpreted cautiously because of publication bias.
8. Survey studies
The survey section appropriately discusses prevalence estimation. However, many HPE surveys investigate associations or compare subgroups rather than estimating prevalence.
The manuscript could briefly distinguish: since these require different sample size approaches.
estimation studies
analytical cross-sectional studies
psychometric surveys
9. Instrument validation
The section would benefit from a stronger emphasis on current COSMIN recommendations.
For example, often influence required sample size more than simple participant-per-item ratios.
factor loading strength
communality
model complexity
10. Attrition
The attrition section is useful.
It may also be helpful to mention: because attrition affects more than simply recruitment targets.
differential attrition
missing data assumptions
multiple imputation
11. Reporting checklist
The reporting recommendations near the end are valuable.
The manuscript could conclude with a concise reporting checklist or flowchart summarizing the required elements of a sample size justification.
Such a figure would likely become one of the most frequently used parts of the paper.
12. Figures
The manuscript currently contains tables but very few visual summaries.
